catalog_quote: Stress is independent of length. It falls on the first syllable of a root in Mary's River and Santiam, remaining there when prefixes are added, although in Tualatin and Yoncalla it is often shifted to the prefixed elements. It is generally accompanied by higher (or sometimes lower) pitch, forming what Jacobs calls pitch accent.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Jacobs 1945 states only the NATURE of the accent, not its PLACEMENT: Santiam (and, per Part III, all Kalapuya dialects in the volume) has a light/weak but definite stress accent that always coincides with slightly higher pitch (an interval of about a second or third above the word's base tone; on long syllabic nuclei the high tone is realized as level tone). No rule for which syllable carries it is given anywhere in the phonetic sections (the texts 'were prepared before intensive study of the phonetics or grammar', p.13); stress is instead marked word by word in the texts with the Americanist acute mark after the stressed vowel (pp.17-81, 89-142 Santiam; 155-198 Tualatin; 204-350 Mary's River; 351-370 Lower McKenzie), so placement is recoverable from the data but is not stated as a rule. Nothing on contrastiveness. Not 'unclear' in the sense of contradiction: the label is used because the work has a stress statement with no placement.
new_statements.exceptions: none on stress. Dialect notes: Tualatin phonemes/variants 'almost entirely as those described for Santiam' except that Santiam's incomplete articulation + weak glottal closure of syllable-final consonants is absent in Tualatin (p.86); geminated/lengthened consonants characteristic of Tualatin are 'phoneme variants determined by syllable weighting', not long phonemes (p.153); Frachtenberg's vowel-length markings in the Gatschet-Frachtenberg texts judged untrustworthy (pp.147, Part III notes).
new_statements.identity_note: The p.15 statement is for Santiam (Central Kalapuya, kala1400; speaker John B. Hudson); the p.152 statement is offered 'roughly for all the dialects noted in this monograph', i.e. Santiam, Mary's River and Lower McKenzie (Central, kala1400) and Tualatin-Yamhill (Northern, tual1242; Gatschet 1877 texts rechecked with Louis Kenoyer 1936); Yoncalla (Southern, yonc1234) is not represented by texts or phonetic remarks. The catalog quote's placement claim (root-initial in Mary's River and Santiam; often shifted to prefixes in Tualatin and Yoncalla) is Hajda's, not Jacobs 1945's.

audit.reasoning: Both deciding passages (Hajda 1976:10; Lewis 2003:3 fn.8 and fn.14 pp.63-64) are held as PDFs with text layers and were confirmed verbatim at the stated pages. The classification (fixed-dominant, root-initial, weight-blind, prefixes unstressed; not in the strict set because no per-length {0,1}^n pattern exists) is exactly what both sources say. Lewis 2003 is the most thorough phonology of this extinct language and is. Glottolog offers nothing better (3 descriptive refs, one of them Banks 2007, held, which is silent on stress placement). The two unheld items (Berman 1990, paywalled; Jacobs 1945, lending-only) are upstream/parallel sources that Lewis already reports as root-initial, so they can refine but not flip the classification. tone.quote: Stress is accompanied generally by higher pitch (sometimes perhaps by lower pitch), which Jacobs calls "pitch accent." He says that pitch accent falls on "every syllable felt to be an independent root--nominal, pronominal, connective, or verbal" (1930: n.p.). ... Frachtenberg records two sorts of pitch: ` (falling) and ~ (rising). ... In some cases it seems to co-occur with stress to form the pitch accent ... Falling pitch is a good deal more frequently marked than is rising pitch. It is probably part of an intonation contour, and the ~ is probably stylistic.
